title: AI Adoption Fails Because We Never Onboard It
author: Joel Salinas and Zohre Shirazi
summary: In this guest collaboration, Joel Salinas frames and Zohre Shirazi of AI Wide Open develops the argument that organizations routinely mistake AI access for AI adoption. Salinas opens with an onboarding analogy: when a person is hired, leaders redesign roles and handoffs around them, but with AI most organizations stop at issuing the badge. Shirazi contends that the real unit of adoption is the workflow rather than the employee, since usage statistics can rise while the underlying process stays exactly the same. She offers a five-layer diagnostic of access, ability, trust, workflow, and ownership, using Klarna's customer service redesign as an example of changing the process rather than a single task. The piece stresses calibrated rather than blind trust and insists that AI never absorbs accountability, which makes naming human owners more important as tools move from recommending to acting. Salinas closes by arguing that ownership is the layer leaders should start with, and a closing FAQ turns the framework into questions for leadership teams.
points: A simple test of real adoption is to ask what would stop working if AI were removed tomorrow; if the answer is almost nothing, the organization has usage but not adoption.
Speeding up one task with AI while collection, handoffs, approvals, and edits stay the same leaves the workflow and the business unchanged.
AI training should start from the work people already do rather than from the tool, asking where AI would make an existing workflow meaningfully better.
Leaders do not need to remove uncertainty but should define what AI can draft, recommend, and what must be checked or approved by a human.
Accountability must be assigned to a named person at the workflow level before decisions are made, because AI does not absorb responsibility.
quotes: We get this wrong the same way we get onboarding wrong. When we hire someone, we don’t hand them a badge and call it finished. We work out what they’ll own, what comes off somebody else’s plate, and where the handoffs move.
Someone can have access to some of the most capable AI tools available and still do their job almost exactly the same way they did before.
And the more I think about it, the more I believe the real unit of AI adoption isn’t the employee.
People are using AI. Usage goes up. Leadership can put the number in a presentation. But if the underlying process hasn’t changed, the business may not have changed either.
That’s the difference between putting AI into work and redesigning work around AI.
If employees don’t trust AI at all, adoption will stall. If they trust it too much, you have a different problem.
AI doesn’t remove accountability. In many cases, it makes the question of accountability more important.
Ask what would stop working if you removed AI tomorrow. If the honest answer is almost nothing, you have usage rather than adoption.
